then.text: Shrews. Like the little furry beasts. We've got plenty of them in the heather.

else.text: SHROOS-bury, of course. Like a shrew. The ponies agree, don't you, Duchess? ... She's eating my map. That's a yes.
The Long Mynd hill ponies have grazed up here for centuries. They belong to the commoners, who have the right to graze the hill, and they're tough as old boots.
Don't feed them. They'll have your sandwiches, your map and your hat.

hills_miner.text: Snailbeach was one of the richest lead mines in Europe once. The Romans had lead out of these hills, and pigs of lead have been found stamped with an emperor's name to prove it.
Lead is heavy, soft and poison. We put it on church roofs and in the water pipes. Now we know better, and the hill is quiet.

then.text: The mist has come down over the Stiperstones. Something huge and patient is sitting in the Devil's Chair, and it turns its head towards you.

else.text: A great jumble of quartzite, shaped very like a throne. Folk say that when the mist comes down, the Devil is sitting in it.

then.text: Stiperstones quartzite! Pale as sugar and hard as a tax bill. Frost split it off the tors in the Ice Age. Have a piece, there's plenty.

else.text: One a day, mind. The Devil counts them.

arts_housman_walker.text: {greeting} I walk with Housman in my pocket. A Shropshire Lad. Sixty-three poems and not one of them longer than a cup of tea.
The joke is that he hardly came here. He grew up in Worcestershire and these hills were the blue line on his horizon. He wrote the whole book from the wrong side of them.
'Into my heart an air that kills, from yon far country blows.' That is the Clee Hills, seen from a schoolboy's window. Cheerful chap. Lovely poems.
